440.name: Brenn
440.history: The second Brenn lies far to the north-east of the first, on a shore of the same shelving rock, and it has the same long ramps of flat stone laid down into deep water. The households of the north-eastern coast began their ramps after those of the northern Brenn had stood a long lifetime, and a third ramp was begun there when two would not serve. Whether the two Brenns were of one people, or only the way of building and the name were carried along the coast from landing to landing, the households themselves could not have said, and did not try. A boy of the landing stood once at the head of the twin ramps on a still evening and watched the water run up the stone and fall back, and asked his mother where the big boats had gone; she told him the sea had them, which was the answer every mother on that coast gave. No hull like those of the first Brenn is remembered to have been built here. At the close of the age the ramps serve small boats and the drying of weed, and some fifty souls live about them, fishing and gathering along the rocks on either hand. The landing lies within a day's rowing of the northern Tarr, and the two keep an eye on one another's smoke.
440.known_for: its twin ramps into the sea

34.name: Tarr
34.history: At the Tarr of the north-eastern headlands a household built a single long house into a cleft of the cliff, with the living rock for its back wall and a roof of turf and driftwood across the cleft's mouth. The hearth stood against the rock, and the rock above it blackened year on year to the height of a man. A child of the house stood with her back to the soot-stain each midwinter to see how far up it her crown reached, until the year she stood as tall as the stain. The house was built for the wind and it kept the wind out: in the hard winter that the whole north-east remembered, when the sea froze in the rock pools and no boat put out from that stretch the whole season, the household lived on what it had put by and came out on the calm morning after with every soul alive. In the darkest months, when the cliff kept the sun from the doorway, a second small fire was kept lit just inside the door, more for its light than its warmth. At the close of the age some thirty souls live in and about the long house and the huts below it, and the stain behind the hearth reaches higher than any of them.
34.known_for: the long house built into the cliff, black with soot behind the hearth

402.name: Tarr
402.province: the north-eastern coast, below the headlands
402.history: The lesser Tarr of the north-east is one of the last landings Seann-Dhaoine made, laid down once the heights were left, when every new work of theirs was made within sight of salt water. It lies on a small inlet below the headlands, a short row along the coast from the older Tarr, and it was settled by households that had outgrown the cleft-house and its huts. Its landing stones are flat slabs set into the shingle at the water's edge, bedded the way the stones of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh in the south-east are bedded, so that a laden boat may be drawn up on them without grinding its hide on the stones beneath. The households fish, gather weed, and trade dried fish along the coast to the older Tarr for what the cliff's shelter can give. At the close of the age it is a landing of a dozen households, young beside its neighbours, and its people still call it by the same root as the landing up the coast, as though the one name were enough for both.
402.known_for: its landing stones, among the last of Seann-Dhaoine' works

404.name: Toll
404.province: the north-eastern coast, in a cleft of the rock
404.history: The north-eastern Toll is a harbour in a cleft of the rock, a narrow inlet between two walls of stone where the sea runs in quiet even when the open water beyond is white. Its households found the cleft in the generations when the rings and Làrach an Dùin-fhaire were still lived in, and made it a landing by cutting the lowest shelf of the rock level with the water, dressing it flat with stone tools over many summers until a boat could lie alongside it and be unloaded dry-shod. The cutting of that shelf is the work the landing is known for, and it is cut in a manner of its own, the face of the rock taken down in long straight strokes. The households are few, fishing the rocks at the cleft's mouth and hunting seal in the season on the skerries to the south. Word of the northern Toll's buried huts came to them along the coast, and they built nothing in the lee of any sand. At the close of the age the landing holds a few households, perhaps forty souls, and its quay is the plainest and most lasting thing on that coast.
404.known_for: its quay cut level in the living rock

97.name: Vell
97.province: the Abhainn bheag, above its mouth in the north-east
97.history: This Vell stands a short way above the mouth of the Abhainn bheag in the north-east, where the ground slopes steeply to the water and each household had to cut its own level ground into the slope before it could raise a wall. Four houses were raised there and a boat-shed, and the households built a flat-bottomed hull for the river that could be poled up the shallows where a sea-boat would ground. A spring flood once reached the boat-shed and lifted the hull off its blocks, and the households hauled it back with ropes and raised the shed a step higher up the slope. The river gave the landing what the open sea further along the coast could not always give: eels in their seasons, trout, and water that never failed. The eel-trap pattern was known only in one pair of hands until an old man taught it to two children at once, lest one bad season lose it to the whole landing. A girl grown up at the Vell stood at the river's mouth one evening looking at the open sea and went no further, holding that a river's own child had no business beyond its mouth. No dwelling of Seann-Dhaoine on the main island is known further to the north-east. At the close of the age some thirty souls live there.
97.known_for: its four houses and boat-shed, the furthest north-east of Seann-Dhaoine' landings

249.name: Tarr
249.province: the eastern coast, under the cut cliff
249.history: The eastern Tarr is a landing under a high cliff of fine grey rock on the eastern coast, and it is the place where the script was first cut. A man of the landing began rows of signs on the standing rock above the shingle with a flint chisel, each sign some two hundred light blows of the hammer, and worked at them a long life; a boy of the landing watched an afternoon of the cutting once and was sent off before he had seen a whole sign made. After the careful cutter, others cut more rows beside and above his, and an old row was cut over and broken by a later hand with the same kind of tool, for what reason the landing never gave. The first row cut on the cliff runs straight and even, and the rows above it less so. The signs are not the speech of the hill-folk, and none of the hill-folk could have read them; the landing's own people say only that the cliff has been cut. A woman of the midland Toll walked the coast once as far as this cliff and found the rows, and went home with nothing to tell but that they were there. At the close of the age some seventy souls live at the landing, fishing the eastern water, and the rows stand pale on the grey rock over their roofs.
249.known_for: the rows of signs cut on the cliff, the first of the script

347.name: Dunn
347.history: The eastern Dunn is where Seann-Dhaoine first leave a trace that can be followed: the great mound of their meals, limpet shell, seal bone and burnt weed, laid down over many lifetimes at the back of the beach until it stood taller than a man. A woman of the landing kept the heap as her mother had taught her, letting each bag of shell fall where the heap wanted it and working it level with her foot, with the burnt weed laid in thin; the heap's fire was kept through a three-day gale by a gatherer whose mother had died at the tide that same season, and she worked a season at the heap alone. An old scraper turned up in the heap one spring, of a shape no one living made, and the household that found it put it back. In time the heap stood high enough that the households climbed it to watch the sea for boats coming home. No tool in the lowest layers is shaped as any tool the hill-folk used. At the close of the age the heap runs the length of the back of the beach and more than a man's height, and the landing below it holds some sixty souls who gather, fish and hunt seal as their mothers did.
347.known_for: the great shell mound, the first sure trace of Seann-Dhaoine

18.name: Dunn
18.province: the Abhainn chaol, a little above its mouth on the south-eastern coast
18.history: This Dunn lies on the Abhainn chaol a little above its mouth, where the river's brown water meets the sea's green, and low cliffs on either hand give nesting to the birds. Its gatherers took eggs from the ledges of those cliffs in the dry months, never so many from one ledge that the birds did not come back to it the next year. It is the northern end of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the lane Seann-Dhaoine' boats kept along the south-east coast in the last lifetimes of the age, from the river mouth below Dunn round the great cape to the bay far to the south. Flat landing-stones were laid along the lane a day's rowing apart, and at Dunn the stones are grooved by keels. A father of the landing taught his son the sea-way stone by stone, naming each landing's look from the water and the look of the sky that meant a boat should lie up there. Rowers on that coast kept a plain word for anyone new to the stretch north of the cape: watch the gulls before you watch the sky. At the close of the age the landing holds some fifty souls and is busier with boats coming and going than its size would suggest.
18.known_for: the head of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh and its grooved landing-stones

186.name: Morn
186.history: Morn lies above a beach on the south-eastern coast, where the catch comes in heavier than the households can eat. Its people built stone-lined pits with short flues above the beach and dried the fish over peat smoke: seven kilns in the end, the first buildings on the island made for a trade and not for sleep or the dead. The fourth pit drowned in a night's rain and was left; the ninth was set higher against the rain; the seventh was the last dug. The keeper of the kilns kept a store of dry peat under an overhang of turf for the kiln fires alone, holding that green peat flares where dry peat smokes and a flare undoes a season's catch, and she taught her niece to watch a kiln past bed on a night of gathering rain. The smoke of the kilns could be seen from inland on a still day. When the heights were left, a household that had lived within the rings came down to Morn, and the keeper of the middle kiln led the son's wife by the wrist to a smouldering kiln and held her hand over its rack until she understood what three tellings in words had not taught her. At the close of the age some sixty souls live there, and the kilns smoke through the summer.
186.known_for: the seven fish-kilns, the first buildings made for a trade

61.name: Cnoc fhionn
61.province: the north-east, in the sheltered hill farms
61.history: Cnoc fhionn, the fair hill, is a hearth-kindred of the hill-folk in the north-east, on sheltered ground under a pale hill with deer forest to the south. Its households were hunters as much as herders, and went south in the autumns to the deer-drives of the eastern woods. Dubhghall, who drove the gully alone for the first time as a young man and took the head of the drive when his uncle's knees failed, lived his last years here. His grandson's dog died the year the boy was eleven, and the boy dug it a grave beside the family's own dead and set a shell at its head. An old woman questioned the grave; the boy's grandfather let it stand; and within a few years two more households of the hill had buried their dogs so. When Dubhghall died, his grandson set a shell at his head too, the last of the small store kept since the dog's grave, saying the old man deserved no less than a dog. Beasts had never had graves on the island before. At the close of the age some fifty souls live at Cnoc fhionn, and their burial ground holds more dogs than any other on the island.
